findings.title: Team administrators are rejected despite the UI permitting them
findings.body: The authorization condition requires `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. Administrator and owner are distinct team roles, so a team administrator who is not also the owner will fail this check and receive FORBIDDEN. The booking list already exposes actions based on `isUserTeamAdminOrOwner`, so team admins can open the dialog but cannot complete the mutation. This should use OR semantics (and ideally the same authorization helper/policy as the booking listing).

findings.title: Attendees are persisted before the external calendar update succeeds
findings.body: The booking attendee records are created before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` is called, with no transaction, rollback, or recovery path. If the calendar update fails (particularly likely when an attendee rather than the organizer initiates the request, since the EventManager is constructed with the caller's credentials), the endpoint returns an error after the guests are already stored. A retry then sees those guests as existing and cannot repair the calendar update, leaving Cal.com, calendar providers, and notifications out of sync.

findings.title: The mutation can add guests to cancelled or completed bookings
findings.body: After loading the booking, the handler authorizes the caller but never verifies that the booking is accepted/upcoming (or otherwise eligible for attendee updates). A caller can invoke this tRPC endpoint directly for a cancelled or past booking and create attendees, update calendar attendees, and send a `CONFIRMED` calendar invitation. This produces misleading invitations and mutates historical/cancelled booking data; eligibility must be enforced server-side rather than relying on the dashboard action visibility.

findings.title: Guest additions have no server-side cardinality limit
findings.body: The public mutation schema accepts an unbounded array of email addresses, and any existing attendee is authorized to invoke it. One request can therefore create an arbitrary number of attendee rows, issue calendar updates, and send invitations/notifications to all supplied recipients (and update emails to existing attendees). This is an email-spam and resource-exhaustion vector independent of the UI; impose a reasonable maximum in the schema and enforce rate/abuse controls.

findings.title: Guest-added notifications ignore event email-disable settings
findings.body: Unlike the other booking notification helpers, `sendAddGuestsEmails` does not accept or check `eventTypeMetadata`, `disableStandardEmails.all.attendee`, or `disableStandardEmails.all.host`. Consequently, adding a guest sends organizer and attendee emails even for event types configured to suppress standard emails. This breaks the event-type notification preference contract and can send mail users explicitly disabled.
